The reproductive biology of Pike silverside Chirostoma estor has been investigated through captive-rearing studies under controlled thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 13.9% [GSI = approximately 13.9%]. This index reflects the relative investment in ovarian tissue and provides a baseline for comparing reproductive allocation among atherinopsid fishes from Mexican lakes. The same thermal regime, maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], also yields a brief incubation period, with the age at birth recorded as 13 days [ab = 13 days] from fertilisation to eclosion. Such a short embryonic phase is consistent with the rapid developmental strategy observed in other members of the Atherinopsidae family that inhabit warm, productive lacustrine environments. Following eclosion, the non-feeding yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first days post-hatching.

Body size parameters for Chirostoma estor indicate a species that attains a relatively modest adult stature within its genus. The ultimate total length is 42 centimeters [Li = 42 centimeters], a dimension that characterises fully grown individuals from Lake Pátzcuaro populations. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight derived from length-weight regressions is 570 grams [Wwi = 570 grams], placing this species among the medium-sized members of the Chirostoma complex. These maximum dimensions are typically achieved after several years of growth in the wild, where seasonal productivity cycles influence annual increments. In comparison, the corresponding length and mass values at the onset of reproductive capability are considerably smaller. The total length at puberty is 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], and the wet weight at puberty is 11.9 grams [Wwp = 11.9 grams], both estimated from the same allometric equation applied to field-collected specimens. This substantial difference between pubertal and ultimate sizes suggests a prolonged period of somatic growth after maturity, a pattern common among iteroparous freshwater teleosts.

Early life stages in Chirostoma estor begin with very small propagules, a trait that influences larval ecology and survival dynamics. The estimated wet weight at birth is 0.0021 grams [Wwb = 0.0021 grams], a value based on the egg diameter of the closely related Leuresthes tenuis and the assumption of spherical egg geometry. Such a minute initial mass places the newly hatched yolk-sac larva among the smallest atherinopsid neonates, with profound implications for feeding ecology during the exotrophic transition. The first exogenous feeding stage must commence within a narrow window after yolk-sac resorption, as the tiny larvae possess limited energy reserves to sustain metabolic demands. Under the constant temperature regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the maximum lifespan is 8 years [am = 8 years], a figure extrapolated from long-term marking studies conducted in the shallow, warm waters of central Mexican highland lakes. This longevity value, spanning nearly a decade, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to the species' ability to persist in variable lacustrine environments.

Comparative analysis of life-history traits reveals that the pubertal length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters] in Chirostoma estor is notably lower than the corresponding values for sympatric congeners, suggesting an earlier onset of reproductive maturation in this species. The wet weight at puberty of 11.9 grams [Wwp = 11.9 grams] similarly falls at the lower end of the range reported for the genus Chirostoma, which includes several species attaining substantially larger sizes before first reproduction. This pattern of early maturity may be an adaptive response to the high predation pressure and seasonal resource fluctuations typical of the shallow, turbid habitats this fish occupies. The ultimate total length of 42 centimeters [Li = 42 centimeters] represents the theoretical asymptotic size derived from growth models fitted to extensive mark-recapture data collected over multiple decades. The ultimate wet weight of 570 grams [Wwi = 570 grams] for Chirostoma estor is reached gradually as individuals approach their asymptotic length, and this maximum mass is typically observed only in the oldest adults. Field surveys indicate that few individuals attain this upper bound due to the combined pressures of fishing mortality and natural predation in Lake Pátzcuaro. Continued monitoring of these life-history parameters is essential for informing sustainable fisheries management in the face of ongoing climatic and anthropogenic pressures on highland lake ecosystems.
